national flag
Mr. LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency):
1.	Is the union jack, national flag of England, also the national flag of Canada?
2.	If so, is the Canadian government taking measures so that Canada may possess a separate national flag?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel I should direct the attention of the hon. member to the wording of his question. It is not so worded as to permit of its being placed on the order paper; nor do I think it is worded in accordance wth what the hon. member himself has in mind. The first part of his question is:
Is the union jack, national flag of England, also the national flag of Canada?
In these words is an assertion that the union jack is the national flag of England. This assertion is not correct. Apart from this, questions on the order paper are not supposed to be placed there for the purpose of making statements or allegations but for the sake of acquiring information. A Scotsman might take exception to the union jack being regarded as the national flag of England^-
We do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, it is the flag of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. I am not doing more than pointing out that circumstance to the hon. member who has asked the question.
The second part of his question reads:
If so, is the Canadian government taking measures so that Canada may possess a separate national flag?
I assume that the word "separate" is not intended to have an invidious significance; it is rather a distinctive national flag I assume the hon. member has in mind. I mention this point because I feel that any attempt to raise a controversial issue over the question of a flag at this particular time would not be calculated to be helpful to the war effort of our country. It is I think desirable not to raise controvers}*- but as far as possible to avoid unnecessary controversy with respect to all matters, whether m relatioh to the answering of questions or, speaking generally, to any other subject that may come up in the house. However, I do not wish to avoid giving an answer to the hon. member which I think will provide the information that the country will wish to have, and which should leave the matter in a position that at least for the present ought to be satisfactory.
A national flag is one which normally is used by a single nation only, and which is used to distinguish that nation from others at international gatherings and to serve as a symbol of it. The red ensign, with the union jack in the first quarter next to the staff, and the Canadian coat of arms in the fly has for



Questions as Orders jor Returns
over seventy years been very generally used in situations where a flag specially distinctive of Canada was essential. It was first authorized by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald shortly after confederation for use on Canadian merchant vessels. Its use as a distinctive emblem on all buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government and situated outside Canada was authorized by order in council on January 26, 1924. It has been popularly accepted as a flag distinctive of Canada.
The union jack, while not a flag distinctive of Canada, may correctly be flown on land in any part of His Majesty's domains.
I question whether this would be a suitable time at which to have parliament determine which particular flag-the union jack, the red ensign or some other flag to be specially designed-should be declared to be the national flag of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I
should like to put a question to the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). In view of the fact that the communist party has been banned in Canada, will the minister allow that
party to hold a national convention on August 21 and 22 next, as announced by the headquarters of the organization?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I was
just about to reply to the question put by the hon. member in my absence last Wednesday and which was couched in terms somewhat different from those he used this afternoon. I quote:
Even though the communist party has been banned by the Minister of Justice, has the minister authorized or will he permit the holding of a national convention by that party on August 21 and 22 next?
The form of the question conferred on the Minister of Justice jurisdiction and authority which he does not enjoy and which he dees not intend to assume. The Canadian communist party was declared an illegal organization by authority of the defence of Canada regulations, and the Minister of Justice has but to apply and carry out the existing regulations. I might add that these regulations have twice been submitted' to the hon. members of the house for examination, and from what I have learned, they were approved and concurred in by the house.
Now, the Minister of Justice has not authorized and cannot allow any organization declared illegal under the defence of Canada regulations to hold a convention or to do anything within the limits of the law.
I think that the hon. member's question was prompted by a news item which appeared in certain newspapers stating that people who had belonged or who still belonged to the group known as the Canadian communist party had announced that they intended to meet-towards the end of August, I believe-for the purpose of laying the foundations of a new political organization. Evidently, the Minister of Justice ' cannot prevent Canadian citizens from calling or holding a meeting for legal purposes. If those who formerly belonged to the communist party, recognizing that the Canadian communist party is banned, now wish to form another group whose constitution, object and actions are not contrary to the provisions of the law, it does not concern the Minister of Justice. If, however, the party were formed with the intention of operating in a manner declared illegal by section 133 of the criminal code, it would be the duty of the attorney-general of each province, on the strength of the responsibility vested in him by the constitution, to prosecute them, and if prosecution seemed to depend on intervention by the Department of Justice, it would not hesitate to

War Appropriation-Supplies
intervene. I should like to recall that, according to section 133, a seditious intention is made manifest by the publication of a document of some kind encouraging, or by otherwise encouraging the use of violence to bring about a change in the set-up of the government of the country. If anyone should attempt to . form a group for the purpose of preaching such ideas, there is not the shadow of a doubt that someone would bring to bear upon it the provisions of the criminal code.

Last week the Minister of Munitions and Supply promised to table certain agreements with the Aluminum company. Is he prepared to do that? Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and SuppljO: I am sorry I cannot table the contract between the Canadian government and the Aluminum Company of Canada because there never has been such a contract. The aluminum is bought by our contractors from the company at a price that has been agreed to by the department and the Aluminum company. The government as such has never bought aluminum from the Aluminum Company of Canada, and therefore there is no agreement.
What about the prices?
I can give you the prices.
The minister said last week that we were paying two cents a pound more than the base price.

The escalator clause for the first quarter of 1942 provided for two cents per pound to all countries; the escalator clause for the second quarter of 1942 provided for three cents a pound; for the third quarter, four cents a pound; for the fourth quarter, four and a half cents a pound and, for the first quarter of 1943, five and a half cents a pound.
As I understand it the base price is fifteen cents a pound, Canadian funds, and that to-day we are paying twenty and a half cents a pound.
That is right, except that fifteen cents is United States funds. The base price in Canadian funds is sixteen cents per pound.

What does the minister mean by escalator clauses if there is no contract?

War Appropriation-Supplies

The escalator clauses apply to the United States and British contracts. They represent the difference in production costs between the basic period-my hon. friend will ask me when the basic period was, but I do not remember; I think it was 1940, and I shall be glad to look it up-and the particular quarter. The amount of escalation represents the differential in the cost of three items, labour, power and transportation.
Is insurance included?
Insurance on transportation, but insurance on plant in Canada would not be an item. Insurance costs bears heavily upon the cost of transportation.
I understood that there were four items in the United States contract.

Perhaps there are. I do not remember what the fourth would be, but I know that labour, power and transportation are the three principal items. There may be a fourth, but it would have only a minor effect. There has been a tremendous increase recently in the cost of transportation. Ships used to come direct from British Guiana to the Saguenay, but now water shipment is limited to a port in the United States, it may be New Orleans, New York or Portland, Maine, and then the cargo is shipped by rail to the Saguenay. Transportation cost has gone up steadily in recent years.

The minister said that the escalator clause to which he referred was in the United States and British contracts. Is the agreement with regard to the price of aluminum governed by the United States and British contracts? If so, does the clause in the United States contract which refers to prices apply to Canadian contracts?

Our contract is for fabricated aluminum, and the price of fabricated aluminum has not been made subject to the escalator clause. It was agreed on some time ago and still stands for our customers. It happens to be the lowest price at which anybody is buying fabricated aluminum in any part of the globe. I think it is lower than the price at which fabricated aluminum is sold in the United States. By fabricated aluminum I mean aluminum sheets, extrusions and aluminum in the form in which it goes into an aeroplane.

Then do I understand that we buy only fabricated aluminum?
Mr. HOW'E: I would not say "only". By "we" I mean the Canadian contractors; I do not mean the Canadian government. I would say that ninety-five per cent of the aluminum our contractors buy is in the form of fabricated aluminum.
Where does the escalator clause come in with regard to fabricated aluminum? The minister quoted a price of five and a half cents a pound over the base price.. Would that apply to virgin aluminum?

That is for aluminum ingots.
Mr. COLDWELL-:	Our contractors are
buying sheet aluminum?
That is right.
And the price of sheet aluminum would be the base price plus five and a half cents?

No. Our purchases are not large, comparatively speaking. I think I can speak with some authority because I went into this matter a short time ago. Our prices have never been made subject to the escalator clause; that is, the prices of fabricated aluminum in Canada have not been made subject to the escalator clause. The escalator clause is written into the contract for ingot aluminum with the United States, Great Britain and Australia. I happen to know of these contracts, because at the moment I am agent for the British government in the carrying out of their contract and it is my duty to check with the auditors. The aluminum is sold to Canadian manufacturers at a price which was agreed upon some time ago and which has never been changed. I assume this is so because in relation to the amount of aluminum sold by the Aluminum company it is not an important matter. So far as I know, there has been no application made to change that price in the last year.
Is that a price per pound, or a price per square foot?
Per pound.
What is the price per pound of the sheet aluminum?
I shall be glad to get that.

We have had some information about these aluminum contracts and I do not rise for the purpose of interfering with the cross-examination of my hon. friend, but in an effort to elucidate the situation if I can. The minister has made certain things very clear. The Canadian government as such does not contract with the
War Appropriation-Supplies

Aluminum company for any production at all, but certain Canadian consumers are buying sheet aluminum from the company. As agent for the British government the minister has a great deal to do with these contracts for the British government. He is their agent; he has told us that. What I want to know is this. With the huge increase in production and consumption the basic unit price has remained more or less constant.
Not at all.
Hold on, now; the basic unit price has remained at about 15 cents, according to my understanding.
What was it at the beginning of the war?
At the beginning of the war-
It was 21J cents.
Oh, yes; less an adjustment made at that time.
The price of aluminum has been reduced with every contract renewal that has been made.
Then let us have that information. That is not my understanding, from the remarks of the minister. Now would the minister allow me to proceed?

Just let me correct this, because I do not like these statements going out all over Canada without being corrected. The cost of aluminum to Canada and her allies has decreased steadily. It was 20 cents in 1940 and 18^ cents in 1941, and it has been 16 cents since July, 1942. That is in Canadian funds.

All right; I am prepared to accept the minister's statement, because he has the facts and I am looking for information. The minister should tell this committee what was the production of the plant prior to 1940; what was the unit price, and what was the unit cost of production prior to the fixing of the price in that year. Then he should tell the committee what the production is now and what the unit cost of production is now. It is my understanding that the production has increased by many times what it was in peace time, and of necessity the cost per unit must have fallen to a very considerable extent. Yet the price has decreased only to the figure just mentioned by the minister, 16 cents, plus whatever increase might be allowed under the escalator clause. I am quite prepared to accept the minister's statement in regard to the increased cost of production

being added to the base price, because anyone who has made a study of the situation knows what the minister said in regard to the increased cost of transportation is in principle absolutely correct. They can no longer transport the bauxite direct from British Guiana to Arvida, as was done before the war; it must come in with a long rail haul from the gulf ports, and that circumstance must have added a substantial amount to the cost of production. But I should like the minister to make clear to the committee and to the country-and I think it would be to the advantage of the Aluminum company-what was the unit cost of production per ton or per pound or whatever unit you wish to use, prior to the war. If the facts are as the minister suggests, he should make this clear to the country. This information must be available to the Department of Munitions and Supply. Then he should state what is the unit cost to-day. I am told that to-day the unit cost is in the vicinity of 5 cents, plus these extras which come under the escalator clause.
Why would my hon. friend make a statement like that? He knows nothing whatever about it, and I can tell him that that is wholly untrue.

The minister need not get hot under the collar; if I am wrong he can correct me, but it seems reason- . able to me, as it must seem to any business man who makes any study of it, that if you have a unit cost pre-war of x dollars and you increase your production by millions of pounds above the pre-war level, the unit cost of necessity must come down. That is what I think the country would like to have some information about.
It must be different from anything else in a war, then.

I have
not a very great knowledge of economics, but I do know that if you produce things on a mass production basis, as compared with a small, peace-time basis, the unit cost ought to fall. That is true in other classes of production, even though the cost of labour has gone up; and the increased cost of labour is taken care of in the escalator clause. All these increased costs are taken care of in the 5i per cent; the minister made that abundantly clear. I am not blaming him for it; I think he should not-I was going to say he should not lose his temper. He did not do that, but he rather quarrelled with the position I was trying to elucidate, by indicating that I was talking nonsense. I am not

War Appropriation-Supplies
talking nonsense; I am asking pertinent questions for the purpose of elucidating the situation.

You are quoting figures
which are not correct.

I beg
the hon. member's pardon; I do not know what he knows about it, but perhaps he will correct us all.

Will you assert that your
statement is true?

No, I do
not know. I have been told, and I am asking the minister for the purpose of obtaining information. I suggest to the hon. member for Parry Sound that I am quite within my rights in doing so; that it is quite a proper thing to do, and that I should not be scolded by him or anyone else for doing so.
What I object to is the hon. gentleman putting the statement on record and into the press that he understands 5 cents is the cost.
Yes, that is my understanding.

The hon. member is quite
in error. He may get that information from fishwives' tales or something, but figures should not be stated in this house unless there is some reason to believe their accuracy.

Well, that is all right; the hon. member has come to the rescue of the minister but I do not think the minister needs any help. He will be able to give us the exact figures and I shall be quite satisfied. I am prepared to accept the minister's statement, but I want an authoritative figure. I think we should have the cost per unit over this period of time together with the pre-war price, the basic price and to-day's price based on the escalator clause. That is a reasonable request. If the unit cost has remained constant in these three years of huge increase in production, then let us know that. I cannot conceive that this should be the case. Anyone engaged in a manufacturing industry knows that if you double, treble, quadruple or multiply your production by one hundred, your unit cost automatically should come down. The minister must have the figures from the chartered accountants or the cost accountants, or some authority, to show just what that position is; and if the minister is prepared to tell me that the price to-day is based on a constant cost price, I am prepared to accept his statement, but I do think the public should
have that information. I am not one of those who joined in the hue and cry against the Aluminum Company of Canada for political purposes.
Oh, no.

No, I
have not, though I think that is one of the main objectives of the hon. gentleman who brought forward this matter.

I rise to a point of
order. The hon. gentleman has no right to impute a motive of that sort to me because I brought this important matter before the house. I may say that there was no political motive behind this.
Oh, oh.
There was an endeavour to serve the best interest of this country which, as I have said before, I think has been sold down the river.

I do not
quite appreciate what the point of order is.

I would rise to
another point of order. This item was passed the last time we considered these estimates, and we are now supposed to be dealing with cargo vessels.
What is your ruling on the point of order, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member for York-Sunbury wishes to speak on the point of order he has the right to do so.

I do not think it is out of order to suggest that a topic was brought up here by the leader of a political party and to say that it was done for political purposes. I do not think that is any reflection on him at all; he would be asleep at the switch if he was trying to make political capital to-day. What was he doing yesterday, the sabbath day, in Montreal, if he was not trying to make political capital; and what was he doing the day before?	-
I rise to a question of privilege. I was not in Montreal on the sabbath day; I was here in Ottawa the entire day. I left the meetings Saturday night.

Then his friends were desecrating the sabbath day by holding a political convention yesterday in Montreal. I accept the hon. member's statement, absolutely, that he was not in Montreal yesterday; and I respect him much for it. But I do suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is not out of order to suggest that a political

War Appropriation-Supplies

party is raising an issue for political purposes. And I just wish to say that I do not join in the hue and cry against the Aluminum company, notwithstanding the fact that I recognize, as I think most of us recognize, that it is one of the greatest monopolies in the world, and that it has come to Canada-I think we will all agree with this-it has come to Canada, notwithstanding the championship of the minister, to escape in a degree the jurisdiction of the United States courts.
Mr. Chairman, what is your ruling on the point of order? The hon. member has concluded his discussion of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the point of order raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Big-gar (Mr. Coldwell) may I say that I understood the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) had accepted the statement of the hon member for Rosetown-Biggar relating to a personal statement.
No, I did not hear him say that. I did not hear him withdraw it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what I heard, if I heard it correctly I thought the hon. member for York-Sunbury had accepted it.
I did not hear that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That there was no ulterior motive so far as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was concerned.
If the hon. member rises and says he withdraws that imputation, that ends it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what I heard.

The basis of my statement was a broadcast statement by a member of this organization, that this was the greatest issue before the Canadian people to-day, and that they were raising it. I am not withdrawing that part of it.
That is a different thing.

If I am out of order the chairman will rule me out of order, and I will accept his ruling. But until he does, may I say I am not imputing any dishonest or improper motives at all, and that is the basis of the rule. To say that a man brings forward an item for the consideration of the House of Commons, parliament and the country, and is doing it for political purposes, is not imputing any improper or dishonest motive.
Yes, it is.
It is quite a proper motive.
What is your ruling, Mr. Chairman?
Before you give your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I think the house should be asked to say what are political motives. What is the definition of a "political motive"?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the point of order, I think the point was well taken by the hon. [DOT]member for Rosetown-Biggar, originally, if there was any motive imputed in the statement made in the House of Commons with respect to the hon. member's actions. But when it comes to be applied to a whole party, then there is no ulterior motive, and there is no point of order.
I am referring to myself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then there was a point of order in that reference,, and I understand the hon. member for York-Sunbury has accepted the statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and has withdrawn that particular statement.
But he has not withdrawn it yet.
What is your complaint?
My complaint is that the hon. member for York-Sunbury said that the leader of this group had introduced this matter of the Aluminum company for political purposes.
Is there anything wrong with that?

I am asking the hon. member to withdraw the imputation. The hon. member for Moose Jaw asked if there is anything wrong with it. Of course there is something wrong. The hon, member is imputing motives to me which are not proper motives-that it was done purely for political motives.
Are you going out of politics?
I deny that I did that.
Perhaps the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will agree that it will have that effect.

To settle this matter I shall be glad to withdraw that remark with respect to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar himself, personally; but I will assert that the political party of which he is the leader has brought forward this topic for political purposes, and for no other purpose.

War Appropriation-Supplies

Mr. Chairman, may I point this out, that the political party of which I am leader did not bring this forward in the House of Commons; the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did. I ask the hon. member to withdraw the imputation, so far as the bringing forward of this matter by me is concerned, and to withdraw unreservedly.

I do not intend to do anything of the kind unless I have to. And I intend to assert that the socialist party in this House of Commons, led by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, has (brought forward this attack on the Aluminum Company of Canada for political purposes, and for no other purposes. And I put mysellf in the judgment of hon. members when I say that.
I say that the party of which I am the leader, through me, brought this forward, if you like, purely in the public interest.
Oh, oh.

Yes, in the public
interest.
Is that political?
And I say that the accusation made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury should be withdrawn, under the rules of the house.

No, no; I want to answer that point of order. It is a fundamental principle of the law of defamation that you cannot defame a political party. You may defame an individual, but you cannot defame a political party.
That may be true of the Progressive Conservative party.

I put myself in the judgment of hon. members of the house when I say it is not defamatory to impute dishonest motives to a political party. If we did, the courts would be full of cases of that kind. But of course it is defamatory to impute dishonest motives to an individual. Surely we have discussed that far enough; I shall now return to the other matters-
May we have a ruling?
If I understand the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar it is that he feels it to be an offence to bring a matter into the house for political purposes.

All right, purely for political purposes. I have always understood politics to mean the business of the nation-the public's business. I have always understood that members of the house are here for political purposes.
But that was not the meaning given to it.

That is a different thing altogether. We have been rather loose in our use of the expression "political purposes", failing to recognize that politics and political purposes are the public business of the nation. We have come to use the word "political" in the sense of partisan politics, every time the word is used. For those who are desirous of destroying our constitutional methods of conducting the political business and political affairs of our country, that of course is the correct interpretation to put upon it, and in that light everything of a political nature should be condemned and scorned. Now, to rule that it is improper to say that a man is bringing an issue before the House of Commons for political purposes would be to convert the meaning of the term "political" into a meaning it never possessed. Surely we are not going to have any such ruling as that. If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar can accuse the hon. member for York-Sunbury of charging him with bringing this matter up for political partisan purposes-
That is what he meant.

and for purely partisan purposes, then I think the point of order would be well taken. But there is no such charge. And no one would have ever thought about it if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had not put that unfortunate interpretation upon it. But I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will not be led into that trap by ruling that we cannot discuss purely political matters in the House of Commons.
We would be out of luck, would we not?

On the point of order, to my mind the definition of politics is the science of the well-being of the people. If that is not our duty in the House of Commons, then I should like to know what it is we are doing here.
Speak for yourself; you cannot speak for the rest of us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have already given my ruling on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I believe the first objection taken by the hon. member was a proper one, because it was supposed to be almost a personal attack as
War Appropriation-Supplies

far aa his political activities were concerned. Then the hon. member for .York-Sunbury withdrew the statement he had made.
No, he did not.
Yes, I did.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The second statement of the hon. member for York-Sunbury was to the effect that the whole party led by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was using the Aluminum company question for political purposes. I believe the point was well taken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) because this is out of the realm of a personal matter. It is a general statement, about a party, and surely we cannot stop an opposition party, or in fact any party, from making a statement of that kind so far as the political party is concerned. I do not believe the rules were ever meant to be applied in that way. I cite standing order 41, citation 297 of Beauchesne's Parliamentaiy Rules and Forms:
The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him, in his turn, of misrepresentation, charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptous or insulting language of any kind; all these are unparliamentary and call for prompt interference.
Again my ruling is that there is no attack, and no point of order, so far as the statement made applies to a party as a whole.

Let me enlighten the membership of this house with regard to the attitude of the political party on this question. I refer hon. members to an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, June 19, entitled "A 'Political Scandal'", which quotes a prominent member of the socialist party in this country, as follows:
For Mrs. Grace Maclnnis, M.L.A., in British Columbia, and wife of Angus Maclnnis, M.P., for Vancouver East, told an Ottawa C.C.F. meeting on Thursday night that "Shipshaw is one of the most valuable pieces of ammunition for the C.C.F. in the forthcoming elections."
Let us strip off all this sham-
I rise, Mr. Chairman-
I have the floor.
May I just say this?
No, you have taken enough of my time.

On a question of
privilege, Mr. Chairman, I was questioning the minister when the hon. member for York-Sunbury rose and interfered with what t was saying, and out of courtesy I sat down.
[The Chairman.]
I have the right to stand and speak.
I have that right too. I rise now just to say that I take no responsibility for statements made by persons other than myself.

I do not intend to follow that further. The whole incident speaks for itself and the Canadian public can judge of it just as well as the members of this house.
I should like the minister to give the committee from the records of his cost accountants, or better still from the records of Price Waterhouse and Company, who are the auditors for Aluminum company, and a reputable firm-make no mistake about that-the unit cost price of aluminum at the beginning of the war and the unit cost price to-day, with a greatly increased production. That will, I think, be illuminating-I am not trying to make a pun. We ought to know if the price being paid for aluminum by the allied governments to-day, with the greatly increased production, is too high. After all, it, is their business. There is, I understand, in all these contracts a provision for renegotiation, and if the unit price to-day is too high I would say that the minister was derelict in his duty if he did not renegotiate that price. But if the unit cost to-day is substantially the same, then the minister has a clearance, and he will have a clearance in the mind of the public too. I am not approaching this thing by way of an attack on the minister at all, and he must not misunderstand me in that respect. If I wanted to make an attack on the Aluminum Company of Canada I could do so. Anybody who wanted to go into the muckraking business could find enough in the aluminum business to stage an attack any time. Just read the history of the Mellon family-you will find it in any standard work in the library-and you will find that the Mellon family and the aluminum business are entangled together. They control a great proportion of the deposits of raw material for aluminum. I have indicated why they came into Canada. There was the question of cheap power. How they got that power is a matter which I think will have to be settled with the government of Quebec; I do not think it is within our jurisdiction to question the terms upon which they got their power, though I have my views on that.
I want to say this further. If the price agreed to be paid by the allied nations at the beginning of the war was not a fair price, that is their responsibility, but the Canadian government has some share in it

War Appropriation-Supplies
even though we are not the direct contractors. If the price paid was fair I do not think there is any great cause for complaint on the part of anybody, because, as the minister said, this material was absolutely essential for carrying on the war, and the Aluminum company has a monopoly, or very largely so, of the production of aluminum. The first consideration in my mind at least has always been and still is the carrying on and winning of the war. But I am going to add this. As the war has proceeded, in other lines of endeavour prices have been reviewed from time to time, and properly so, with a view to cutting down costs of these essential materials required for the manufacture of aeroplanes and other war munitions. It will not do for the minister to say, as I think he did say, and I do not agree with him in that attitude: Oh well, we get it all back in taxation.
I did not say that at all.
That is the effect of what the minister said.
Never.

Well, the company is making a lot of money and it is paying huge sums in taxation. But on the other hand this government has agreed to give to a subsidiary of this company a generous depreciation allowance, to say nothing else, and I think I could go a good deal further than that. But what I would like to know from the minister is the basic unit cosfi-
You have said that four times already.

Then I
will say it five times because I am thinking of the taxpayers of this country. I want to . know from the minister what the basic cost was pre-war, then at the beginning of the war, and in each year of the war. If the minister will give us those figures substantiated by the certificates of his chartered accountants, I shall not have another word to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understood that when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar rose this afternoon it was to ask a question, on which he had been promised an answer from the Minister of Munitions and Supply. We have dealt with the activities of the Aluminum company at great length on previous occasions. We are now on item 2, dealing with cargo vessels. I think I am expressing the desire of the committee generally when I say that we should stick to the item before us; otherwise it will be impossible to make that progress
which the committee and the country expects. The committee has already had a lengthy and fairly thorough discussion.
I rose to ask the minister to table some documents which he had promised.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The Chairman said that you were in order.

I did not hear his remarks. May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the record is there. The Aluminum company stated that including the profits of the bauxite and power companies the cost of production in 1938 was 8-93 cents, *when the plant was operating at only 50 per cent capacity. In 1929 the company got a price of thirteen cents, for 75,000,000 pounds.

That is
what they sold for? It is not the cost.

Yes, that is the selling price of the article. The hon. member for York-Sunbury spoke of a price of five cents. To be perfectly fair about it the price quoted to me, and I was cautioned that with the usual terms of amortization-and the terms are unusual now

which would enter into the cost of production the price would be in the neighbourhood of six cents a pound. But as I said the other day, I had no figures to substantiate that although it was given to me by somebody who I thought would know what he was talking about.

Mr. Chairman, just to show
how far afield hon. gentlemen are, I will give the production figures of the Aluminum company for the years beginning with 1939. In 1939 Aluminum company produced 82,800 short tons of aluminum; in 1940 the production was 109,200 short tons; in 1941, 212,300 short tons; in 1942, 335,800 short tons; and it is estimated that this year the company will produce 503,000 short tons, or over 600 per cent of the production in 1939, which was Capacity production.
I might say that I am the custodian of the British contracts in Canada at the present time. That is a confidential mission which I have. I was appointed agent of the British government with the distinct understanding that I would not disclose any contracts that I made on behalf of the British government or any facts which I obtained in that connection.
I have followed very carefully the costs of producing aluminum, and I am satisfied that the price has been kept in a reasonable relation thereto. The British government, having all the facts, have come to the same conclusion; at least I have heard no complaints. So
War Appropriation-Supplies

far as the government of the United States, the other large customer of the Aluminum company, is concerned, they have direct contractual relations with the Aluminum Company of Canada. I am not associated with that contract in any way, but I assume that there again relations are satisfactory. As to price of fabricated aluminum that is purchased by Canadian contractors, I know about that, and I am satisfied that that is a fair and reasonable price.
My hon. friend said that he thought the cost of manufacturing aluminum was five cents a pound. The profits of the Aluminum company, or Aluminum Limited, which incidentally include the profits from a number of operations outside Canada, are known every year; they are published. My hon. friend reasons that, forgetting the escalator clause, if the cost of producing aluminum is five cents on a prewar basis the profit would be eleven cents.
No, I said I thought to-day the cost was five cents-not pre-war.

The hon. member says that the cost is five cents. Well, the cost, of course, would take all factors of cost, including the increased costs appearing in the escalator clause. But I say, drop that out, go back to the unit costs of pre-war, the cost of labour, of power, and transportation; if these are assumed, on that basis the suggestion is that aluminum can be produced for five cents a pound, and the profit would represent eleven cents a pound. If the hon. gentleman will check the profits per pound on the tonnage of aluminum I have given him, against the balance sheet of the company, he will see that he is very far afield indeed in his assumptions of cost. I am afraid that is all the information I can give him.

Let us
understand the situation. The minister says that because of his financial relationship with the British government he is not able to reveal the figures of cost of production. I would not quarrel with the minister for taking that attitude so far as the British government is concerned; but in his capacity of minister of munitions and in view of his familiarity with the contracts for Canadian consumption in a semi-processed state, possibly that secrecy would: not obtain. Now if the minister has said-and he has in effect said

that because of his commitments to the British government he is not able to give us the real cost, I am not going to ask him to break his plighted word to the British government, because after 
all it is their responsibility and their business, and their money is paying for this. But what has been bothering me all along, in reading the discussion, including the speeches of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar here and outside the house, and the minister's reply, is this, that if the production is increased by 600 per cent the unit cost must have fallen very substantially, and the taxpayers, not only of Canada but of the United States and Great Britain, should have had the benefit. That is the only point I desire to make. If I am wrong in my assumption, why, I am wrong. I may say to the minister that the figure which was quoted to me was given by a man who said that he knew something about the aluminum business. I am free to tell the minister that I cannot adduce proof in support of that five cents a pound; if I had it I would produce it; make no mistake about that; I would have been camping on the minister's trail a good while ago. I rose for purposes of gaining information and an explanation as to why, if production has been increased 600 per cent, the price has not gone down. We have not had an answer on that, and apparently we are not to get it.
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend cannot assume that because volume goes up prices necessarily go down.
The base price-with the escalator clause.
The base price has gone down, of course. Nevertheless the freight per ton on bauxite is the same for a million tons as it is for a hundred thousand.
Oh, but you cover that in the five and a half cents.

I am not talking of the war increase. I say, had prices remained stable the cost of transporting bauxite, which was a large operation before the war, would not have changed materially for an operation six times the size. The cost of transportation would not have changed, nor would the cost of power. It takes so many kilowatts of power to smelt one pound of aluminum, and the price per kilowatt hour is usually a constant price. Any saving will have been in labour, through the larger operation, and the distribution of overhead, and I think the reductions in the base price which have been made take care of that item.
I have watched this situation very carefully. I have taken into account the obligations of the Aluminum company-obligations taken on in the interests of winning the war, and with my approval-and I am satisfied

War Appropriation-Supplies
that the price of the aluminum contracts today is a reasonable price, and one which does not allow an undue margin to the shareholders of the Aluminum company after their obligations have been discharged.

May I ask the minister a question about the transportation of bauxite? I read an item a few days ago to the effect that it is being landed at New Orleans, transported by canal boats up the Mississippi to the Ohio canal, thence through the Ohio canal to a final connection, I assume the Erie canal, and down the St. Lawrence river by boat to the Saguenay.
Did my hon. friend in his travels ever cover that route?
Does it go by canal boat or by rail?

It goes almost every other way, and in almost every kind of boat, including canal boats, but it does not go up the Mississippi river. My hon. friend would not expect it to go through the Chicago barge canal, which is hardly a route.
It has a nine-foot draft.
Hardly that. About six feet, on the Mississippi.
No. Chicago has a nine-foot draught.

It has never gone that way. As a matter of fact it has gone by rail from gulf ports. A certain amount comes from New York up the barge canal to Oswego, where it is transhipped and brought down to the Saguenay by boat.
The barges on the Mississippi are 500-ton barges. They have a nine-foot draft. They come up the Ohio river.

I think we can arrive at some idea of what is going on by looking at page 3631 of Hansard where, in the table given on that page, there is an item, "Provision for depreciation and depletion." There is another item giving the net profit of Aluminium Limited for the year transferred to earned surplus. The total of the two items is $56,870,784. The minister has given the number of pounds involved in this, and if you allow for the normal depletion you can arrive at what the profit per pound is.
After excluding earnings of a number of other companies.
The major portion is earned by the Aluminum Company of Canada.

One other question with respect to the effect of the escalator clause. The minister said that the amount of adjustment in the first quarter of this year was 5i cents. That, added to the 15 cent base rate, meant that the American government was paying 20i cents. The question I wish to ask with respect to the 20 per cent of the contract which was being paid for at the rate of 17 cents per pound, according to the letter which Mr. Jesse H. Jones wrote to Senator Truman on March 24, is this: Does this mean that the American government is paying 22\ cents for twenty per cent of the aluminum purchased?
No, it does not mean that.

I wish to ask a question with regard to information given to the press to the effect that Austin C. Taylor of Vancouver had been appointed special representative of D. W. Ambridge, director-general of the naval shipbuilding branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Are there two branches, one for the building of cargo boats and one for the naval shipbuilding branch, and does Mr. Taylor represent Mr. Ambridge or the minister of munitions in Vancouver? The article states that he represents Mr. Ambridge. I always thought that when a man was appointed he represented the government, but according to this item Mr. Taylor represents Mr. Ambridge. Will the minister give the house some particulars with regard to the naval shipbuilding branch and the appointment of Mr. Taylor?

The merchant shipbuilding programme is under the supervision of wartime Merchant Shipping Limited, of which Mr. H. R. MacMillan is president and Mr. Austin Taylor vice-president in charge of operations of the west coast. All other shipbuilding is under the naval shipbuilding branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply, of which Mr. Douglas Ambridge is director-general. The branch has only one large shipyard on the Pacific coast, namely, Yarrows Limited, whereas Wartime Merchant Shipping have, I believe, five large operations in the Vancouver area. It was felt that in the naval activities there, having to do with Yarrows Limited, one shipyard could be better coordinated under the direction of Mr. Taylor, who would thus have the whole steel shipbuilding industry on the Pacific coast under his responsibility. It was considered that a more equitable distribution of labour and a better servicing would result from Mr. Ambridge's delegating his responsibilities on the Pacific coast, in regard to steel shipbuild-
3S38
War Appropriation-Supplies

ing, to Mr. Taylor, who will report to Mr. Ambridge as far as naval shipbuilding is concerned.
What has become of Mr. Desmond Clarke?
He has changed his position. He is now assistant to myself in charge of certain special duties.

In connection with the building of cargo vessels and the like, it is said that the increase in expenditures during the coming year will be approximately 300 per cent over the figure to-day. I would ask the minister to advise the committee how many men are to-day employed in cargo shipbuilding, how many men will be required during the next year in the expansion of the present programme, what measures are being taken to recruit the necessary man-power for this particularly specialized type of work, and what assistance the selective service authorities are giving the minister in securing the necessary man-power.

So far as merchant shipbuilding is concerned, my hon. friend will understand that the appropriation before the committee is in payment for that portion of the ships we build that will be operated by Park Steamship Limited. They are being called up if they are in the proper age groups. I made the statement the other day that at this stage we are making no demands on the army, navy or air force for the deferment of any man unless he has a very unusual skill which we cannot obtain otherwise at this time.

The ships are insured against what is called "P and I", that is protection
and indemnity. They are not insured against war risk; but they are insured against a third party risk. The administration deserves credit for recognizing that the amount of housing available for the people of the country will directly affect the production of munitions. I have in my hand a copy of the brief presented to the committee on reconstruction and re-establishment by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, in which reference is made to the serious housing shortage in Canada as revealed by the 1941 census. One statement is to the effect that twenty-five Canadian cities with populations of over thirty thousand reported that sixty-one per cent of their people lived in rented quarters. Of these tenants 53-6 per cent paid less than $25 a month rent, 36-3 per cent paid less than $20 and 16-5 per cent less than $15. More than 17 per cent of the houses had neither bath nor shower, while 30 per cent had no means of refrigeration, either mechanical or by ice. In mentioning this very serious situation the brief goes on to state that in the city of Hull, for example, 25 per cent of the houses are in the category of those for which the rental is less than $15. Anyone who has had any experience in looking for housing accommodation in Canadian cities can picture the sort of quarters available at $15 per month. The mayors' association made some valuable recommendations, which I shall discuss a little later.
The bureau of statistics reports that urban centres would require 143,314 new housing units to give each family a separate unit; and the estimate of the family units required in rural Canada shows that 82,612 units would be required to provide separate family units. The total number of houses required to give each family in Canada a separate unit would be something over 225,000. In view of this very serious shortage one might anticipate that Wartime Housing Limited could embark upon an ambitious house-building programme without creating a surplus of houses for the post-war period.
I have some reports from typical Canadian cities to which I should like to refer; one very illuminating report deals with the city of Ottawa. Atlee wrote the Halifax Chronicle on Wednesday, June 4, 1941, after the hon. member had made his comments here, and in his letter he said:
Your columns this morning contain the information that Mr. M. J, Coldwell has been "censured in some quarters" for bringing to public attention the condition of the slums of this city. Surely this represents ostrichism in its blatant and unabashed form-that ostrichism which, head hidden in the sand, declares that the thing it does not want to see should not be seen even by more intelligent birds. Mr. Cold-well made no extravagant statement about our slums. No statement could be couched too extravagantly to describe their loathsome squalor. I have worked in the east end of London and in some of the less salubrious environs of Manchester, and I saw nothing there any worse than exists in Halifax. Our slums are a disgrace and a shame to us-a disgrace abounding and a shame reproaching. In tolerating them we have shown a criminal indifference. For they are more than a shame and a disgrace; they are a cancer, eating into our very life and health.
A report from Winnipeg covering the year 1942 states:
. . . it will be seen that we have reached an all-time low in the number of vacancies, which means that more and more families are having to crowd together. This condition is, of course, in conflict with our health and other by-laws, but it is evident that there is little we can do about it. . . .
The shortage of accommodation for the low-income group has been acute for years and I have referred to this over and over again in these reports. The present plight of the average working man to find moderate but satisfactory living quarters for his family is lamentable. . . .
Surely our present housing shortage cannot continue much longer. The risk to health of our sub-standard housing, not to mention that of the fire hazard in our nondescript tenements, may be brought home to us with painful remorse. My attention has been drawn to a report appearing in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of

I have seen the slums of London and our eastern cities, but I have never seen the abject poverty and want that exists among the settlers of northern Saskatchewan.
In the past, as those responsible for the affairs of our country, we have not faced up to the cost of maintaining these slums. I have here a report on municipal housing by Helen Alfred of the national public housing conference of the United States, in which she says:
American slums are among the worst in the western world. From coast to coast, from Canada to the gulf, the housing conditions which families in the lower income brackets are obliged to occupy are a shocking commentary on what we like to call the American standard of living. Toward no other form of economic maladjustment have we remained more archaic in our attitudes, less progressive in action. While imagination, skill and boldness have marked the attack of American cities on problems of health, education and recreation, the housing problem-the inability of low-income wage workers to secure homes of modern standard at rents within their means, has been treated w-ith vacillation, subterfuges or complete indifference.
A study was made in Winnipeg back in 1935 in regard to the cost to the taxpayers of that city of maintaining their slums. They took into account the cost to municipal hospitals, social welfare agencies, the police department, the children's aid society, the children's bureau, the Winnipeg general hospital and the St. Boniface outdoor clinic, and compared the cost in the worst slum area with the cost in the rest of the city. They found that in this worst slum area the cost of maintenance amounted to $639,000. Had the cost in that area been at the same rate as in the rest of the city it would have amounted to only $189,000, showing a difference of $450,000. In other words it cost the taxpayers of the city of Winnipeg, the gateway to the west, nearly half a million dollars to maintain the slums of that city.
The special committee of this house which investigated housing in 1935 reported that a survey made in Cleveland indicated that where 2J per cent of the population lived, 22 per cent of the murders were committed, 6-8 per cent of juvenile delinquency existed and 121 per cent of deaths from tuberculosis occurred. Although the per capita cost of fire protection in Cleveland is only $3.12, the cost in the slum area is $18.12. The estimate for the total cost of the slum area is $1,740,000.
I mention these two or three specific cases to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the creation and maintenance of a slum area is a costly business. Unfortunately I am afraid that as part of our war-time housing programme we are building some new slum areas. Wartime Housing Limited deserves credit for entering the field fairly early in the war. Houses have been provided in a number of areas, where, had they not been built, there would have been a serious shortage of housing accommodation. I am quite prepared to admit that the houses which have been built by Wartime Housing Limited are superior to a great many other houses found in cities in which there is overcrowding. But I come back to the point I made a year ago, that many of the temporary houses being built by Wartime Housing Limited will be the slums of to-morrow. The taxpayers of Canada have spent a large sum of money to build houses. I am not complaining about the amount of money spent for this purpose. When one considers that this year the Minister of Munitions and Supply will supervise the expenditure of $3,400,000,000, the fairly modest estimate of $30,000,000 for housing seems like a small sum indeed. But as a taxpayer I am concerned that the people should receive good value for these houses. I am also concerned that houses which will be slums in a few years should not be built in areas in which a permanent housing shortage exists.

Adequate housing is a morale builder and is essential to the speed and efficiency of our national defence work.
The programme of clearing slums and providing decent homes for the ill-housed of our nation in the years before the war laid the foundation for the intensified housing effort necessary to-day. The job of clearing the slums, which your Conference helped to begin, of necessity must be reduced substantially for the duration. With the scarcity of building materials we can now afford to build homes only in defence areas. But the goal of a slumless America must be preserved. ...
I have also the report of a speech delivered recently in the United States by the Hon. Walter Nash, who was the sponsor of a housing bill in New Zealand in years before the war. He said.
We simply cannot afford to pay the tremen-clous price we have paid in the past by leaving such matters in the hands of those who acknowledge no social responsibility. We cannot afford to leave the way clear in the future for the predatory activities of the speculator, with the repetition of the muddle and the waste that must always result from unplanned development.
There is the problem, too, of considering housing in its proper relationship to other phases of general regional planning. Industry and housing, for example, must be considered

for planning purposes as two parts of a single problem. A building project no longer involves merely the construction of a number of dwellings. The larger the scale of operations, the more we are compelled to pass from purely constructional fields into fields which embrace almost every phase of communal activity. When we commence to plan for housing, on any national scale, we are in effect planning for the future of the nation.
I have two or three illustrated booklets telling what remarkable progress has been made in New Zealand under a labour government in connection with the building of suitable homes for every family. I should like to draw the attention of the committee to an interesting little book entitled "Homes or Hovels", recently published by the Canadian Association for Adult Education and the Canadian Institute of International Affairs. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) is honoured in having a sketch of himself in it. The hon. member made a telling address at the conference held in Toronto sponsored by the Ontario Association of Architects, that provided the material for this book. It is encouraging to find a representative group from various parts of Ontario showing the initiative to bring Catherine Bauer, who is without doubt one of the best of the English-speaking authorities on housing. I suggest that hon. members secure a copy of this valuable booklet and become familiar with the suggestions.

Recently the mayor of Toronto, accompanied by some members of the council, interviewed the minister and the head of Wartime Housing Limited. I am sure the minister will readily admit that the requests of the city of Toronto were reasonable and were presented in a businesslike manner and supported by a well prepared brief. I shall occupy only a few moments, but I intend to read a few paragraphs of the brief, because they clearly indicate what that great city is up against, and how the city itself has tried to help the minister with a problem which now confronts him; for he has been up against a serious problem, and I for one think he has made the best effort he can to solve it. On May 13, Toronto, through the .mayor, presented a brief in which a number of reasons are stated to show why the city requires assistance in handling the serious housing problem that exists there. The first clause on page 1 reads:
We would draw to your attention the housing situation that has been created in Toronto by the great influx of people from other sections
of Canada to accept employment in the armament and munition plants located both in the city proper and in the adjacent municipalities.
I might add that immediately north of the city in York township, east of the city in East York and west of the city in West York, many thousands of people reside, a great many of whom work in the city while living in the townships or in the adjacent municipalities, and these municipalities too are congested. They have their housing problem, and for that reason the city honoured them by referring to the equal difficulties with which they are faced. The city itself tried to overcome these difficulties and to help out the minister and his board, first, by making a tabulation of vacant stores throughout the city, and with the consent of the board such stores as could be converted into dwellings were so utilized to the number of 225. But that quickly exhausted the available number of stores which could be turned into dwellings. Some of them are in my own end of the city, and while they are not all that could be desired, they do assist in overcoming the temporary difficulty that exists in consequence of inadequate accommodation. The city then made application to the board, and here I will read what the brief says:
The civic administration has conferred on several occasions with officers of Wartime Housing Limited. At a recent meeting with Mr. J. M. Pigott and Mr. V. T. Goggin, we presented the city's application for the erection of 300 houses on land provided by the city, 200 of which would be available for war workers' families certified as such, 100 for families of soldiers overseas, and civilians, this latter group to be erected and operated under a similar plan to that provided in the city of Halifax.
The difficulty is that soldiers' families have been particularly affected by the lack of accommodation. For some reason or another, which I do not consider warranted, many landlords have refused to accept soldier tenants. I have a number of them myself and I find them very satisfactory. In fact, I could have rented the buildings for much more, but I would not be guilty of turning out a soldier's wife and family, particularly when he is overseas defending, not only myself, but everybody else. However, everybody does not treat them in that way, and therefore we have a serious problem-. To continue with the brief:
We were advised that directions respecting housing for war workers should emanate from the Department of Munitions and Supply and for those coming within the other groups from the Department of Finance, or more directly the national administrator of real property.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with regard to wartime housing as it exists in Halifax. I did not intend to take part in this discussion except that my name was drawn into it by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). He was referring to the difference of opinion which had existed between the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and myself two years ago, but I do not know that that has any great bearing upon the item we are discussing of $30,000,000 for housing development. I wish to approach this question in the same reasonable manner as that of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). The hon. member asked the minister to consider the problem they have in Toronto and he presented a reasonable case. I am sure that the minister will give consideration to this problem. I propose to approach the minister with the same thought in mind.
For at least two years the hon. member for Mackenzie has been dealing with this question of housing, but it has always been in a critical mood, he has been criticizing expenditures, overhead, stating that costs were excessive and so on. I have studied the figures he has given from time to time, as well as those presented by others who were supposed to know. The chairman of the wartime housing board gave definite figures and I am sure he had available the costs of the various units.
This is a very large project, one which has been developed during the past twenty-eight months. Practically nothing had been done when the board was appointed in February, 1941, but they gathered together the best
architects in Canada, drew up plans and decided on the types of home which would best meet the emergency. We are faced at the present time with a shortage of houses, brought about largely by the needs of war workers who have gone to the urban centres. Steps were taken to provide suitable homes of a temporary nature for these workers. Instead of being critical of the Minister of Munitions and Supply for the efforts he has made, I think we should realize that this project has been handled in a splendid manner. I realize that he has not been able to give all centres the number of houses they have asked for, but an effort has been made to meet the situation.
In Halifax attempts have been made from time to time to meet this problem. We approached the minister with the request that something like 600 houses should be erected. This would be in addition to the 1,400 to 1,500 houses which had been erected in and around Halifax. In Canada since December 1, 1942, a total of 17,441 houses, 93 staff houses, 10 dining houses, and 32 special buildings such as administrative buildings and recreation centres have been erected by the government at a total cost of something like $70,000,000. With these figures before us we realize what a large undertaking this has been. When we consider the large number of units that have been erected and the small number of complaints that have been made, I think we must agree that the Minister of Munitions and Supply should be congratulated upon the able manner in which he and Wartime Housing Limited have carried out this project.
I do not know which set of figures is correct, but I have in my hand a copy of an article which appeared in the Canadian Editorial Digest and which gives the average cost of the houses erected to date throughout Canada as $1,959. For the province of Ontario the average cost was $1,927, and for the city of Hull, to which the hon. member for Mackenzie has referred so often, the average was $1,889, as against the figure of $2,869 which the hon. member quoted.
What is the hon. member reading from?

I am giving the figures shown in the Canadian Editorial Digest, and I believe a magazine of this kind would make sure of its figures. It goes into the development of the whole scheme in a thorough, businesslike way; it states the number of houses erected and so on, and then gives the average cost. I am not going to say anything further on that point except that these figures certainly are quite different from those given by the hon. member for Mackenzie.

Would the hon. member permit a question?
I sat quietly and listened to the hon. member, but I shall be pleased to answer his question.

I wonder if the hon. member would believe the figures if he saw them in the contracts. I have them here, and the contract price is given as $2,705, according to a return brought down a year ago. I shall be glad to send them over to the hon. member, and I feel sure he will accept these figures.

I am quite prepared to accept the hon. member's word that the figures he has quoted were given in a return. I am simply stating the average cost of these homes throughout Canada, and particularly in the province of Ontario and the city of Hull. As a business man naturally I would want to go into these figures which the hon. member has kindly sent over to me, in order to see whether they cover simply the cost of construction or take in other items as well. Perhaps the hon. member for Mackenzie may not have gone into all the factors as closely as he might. Recently the hon. gentleman was good enough to pay a visit to the city of Halifax. I would not, of course, think he went there for political reasons at all, at a time such as this; but with all the publicity the hon. member has obtained through his criticism of Wartime Housing; in spite of the fact that he stayed in Halifax for a few days-and I hope he enjoyed himself while there-and the fact that he was going to speak there, I venture to suggest that he was not waited upon by a delegation of tenants from the wartime houses to lodge a protest. I would go farther and venture to suggest that he did not receive ten individual protests during the time he was in Halifax, or in fact that he did not receive three protests during his stay in that city. If I am correct in my assumptions; if he did not receive any protests following the erection of 1.500 homes in that city, I say the houses built under this scheme must be carrying out the purpose for which they were intended, namely, to house the war workers and others who were brought to Halifax for a particular purpose.
Naturally I am concerned about the situation in Halifax. I want to see more houses there; I think we need more houses, and I ask the minister to give serious consideration to the erection of more homes in that city. The situation that exists in Halifax to-day has been brought about by the fact that Halifax has become a national port, and there has been an influx of an additional twenty-five to thirty-five thousand people. The hon. member referred to the building of new slums.
[Mr. Xsnor.l
I doubt if any reasonable member who studied the lay-out of that new section, who saw the care that was taken, who looked into the general construction of the homes and observed the general surroundings, would say that we were building new slums in the construction of these wartime houses. I think his statement is a very unfair one to make, and I do not think it will help us in meeting the housing situation as we are endeavouring to do at the present time. I quite agree with the hon. member as to the desirability of permanent basements and solid walls; I emphasized those points when the city of Halifax made application for the additional 600 houses to which I have referred. I suggested that they should be of a little better type and should be constructed in sections of the city which would give a greater resale value when the time came to dispose of them. I believe if the houses could be of a better type, with permanent basements or with provision for the addition of permanent basements later on, not only would it add to the resale or salvage value of the houses, but it would give the people now ocupying them something permanent which they could call their own, thus helping to make them better citizens.
Then the hon. member referred to children kicking holes in the walls. Well, if he would examine the walls of these houses, as I have examined them on more than one occasion, he would not make that statement. A child could no more kick a hole in a wall of that type than in any other wall. The hon. member also said that the overhead is high. He did not elaborate on that point; he did not say what he meant by the overhead, whether it was overhead in connection with the operation or the upkeep. My information is to the contrary, that the overhead is particularly low, as it should be at the present time. We should not have any real depreciation or expenses in connection with repairs to these houses for some four or five years. I do not think the cost of upkeep is a bit higher on a percentage basis than in connection with any other type of construction. It is all very well for us to find fault with efforts of this * kind. We can all be critical, but it takes really constructive ability to plan a venture like this, running into $70,000,000. A few mistakes are bound to be made, perhaps in selecting the type of house, or something of that kind. Perhaps the hon. member had in mind something of a more permanent nature, but that could not be undertaken on this basis because the cost would have been very much greater.

War Appropriation-Supplies-Housing
Then the hon. member mentioned houses built with an investment of $750. That was under national housing. The people who are occupying these prefabricated houses are not in a position to make an initial payment of anything like $750 or $500 or even $350. They are temporary employees carrying on war work. No doubt Wartime Housing had that in mind when they built houses of this type to accommodate people of this kind. Even if some of these people had $750 in their [DOT] pockets or in savings accounts, I doubt whether they would want to invest it in houses in the section in which they are now living. So that I say the national housing scheme and the wartime housing development are entirely different. Personally I favour the national housing scheme for permanent homes, except that it should start at a lower figure. I am hopefully looking forward to the day when once again we shall have a measure operating in full force throughout the dominion, and when again we shall have an opportunity to invest and to build homes along the lines laid down by the national housing scheme.
Then the hon. member criticized the Minister of Munitions and Supply for not meeting his request to supply hon. members with a plan. I cannot recall the details, but if I remember correctly that was a plan which had not yet been approved or released. In the same breath the hon, member asked why Wartime Housing did not do the same as the national housing authorities had done, and encourage the people to send for plans. I believe the encouragement given by the national housing authorities was to select a plan which could be purchased for $10.
They had plenty of free ones.
One could look at plan 10, 11 or 12, or whichever plan he wished, and then he would pay $10 to procure a copy of it. That is quite different from the idea expressed by the hon. member.
Would the hon. member suggest that the national housing authorities would not produce specifications for any member of the house?

I am not suggesting anything. I am just stating the facts as they exist, and explaining away some of the misconceptions which might arise from the speech of the hon. member. I could say, "We will send to National Housing and procure a set of plans and specifications." We could not get them from Wartime Housing. They are
two different things, and they must be approached in a different way.
I have spoken longer than I intended, but I do not wish to lose the opportunity of saying a word respecting the situation in Halifax. Certain groups in that city have organized meetings and passed resolutions which have been sent to the minister. This action has been taken by the city council, and by other social agencies. The minister has given sympathetic consideration and kind attention to the requests made. Some time ago he met a deputation from Halifax, and asked how many houses were required. I believe he was told that at that time the city would require 600 houses. He said, "Well, go ahead with 400, and after you have completed them you may come back and we shall see what can be done about the other 200." The big problem in Halifax, one which no doubt exists in other places, is that the city could not quickly provide suitable sites to take care of 400 houses. The result is that to-day we have only 225 of those 400 houses. So that it is not altogether the fault of Wartime Housing Limited or the Minister of Munitions and Supply that we have not sufficient housing in Halifax.
I would ask that the minister give favourable consideration not only to the recently expressed request for the speeding up of the building of the remaining number of houses, but that fire protection for those houses should be arranged. Fire protection in Halifax involves a heavy additional outlay, owing to the increased population in the city, and the additional number of war-time buildings which have been erected. Then, more police protection is required. While I do not wish to introduce another factor for the consideration of Wartime Housing Limited, still I must urge that fire protection and police protection for these homes are matters closely connected with any building scheme, and I would ask the minister to consider the providing of a lump sum to defray expenses entailed by those increased responsibilities.
There is another subject, namely, that of health protection, which I would bring to the attention of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, nearly every war-time house at the present time has a victory garden. Throughout the country, wherever there are war-time
