houses, community houses have also been put in, and they have been of great help. The people who live in the war-time houses have had meetings in these community houses, and after their day's work the men who work sometimes from seven in the morning until six at night, and perhaps go back for a while to work after supper, and work even on Sundays, have in their spare time cultivated victory gardens. In Peterborough, the city which I represent, some families moved into one section on the first of June and immediately began to cultivate victory gardens. They planted their seeds, and last week were pleased to see that the potatoes were coming up and that the lettuce, radishes and carrots would be ready, too, perhaps this week. Then, without any notice whatsoever to these people, Wartime Housing comes along and planks sheds right down on these victory gardens, tramping the lettuce, radishes and potatoes right into the ground. That was a shame. I know the minister is not to blame for it, nor is the president of Wartime Housing, but somebody is to blame for it. The people who have tended these gardens are mad. A man who telephoned me about it started out by saying, " Now, Gordon, if these telephone wires burn up before I get this thing off my chest I want you to call around and see me on the way to your train." He asked me what I would do if I had been one of these men. I hesitate to say in this house what I would have done. These people are naturally very much upset over it all, and I feel that Wartime Housing, the president of which was here to-day, should see to it that these sheds are not put on these victory gardens without the consent of these people. It is worse than sacrilege to tramp down a man's garden after he has spent hours and hours digging and cultivating it; it is just as bad as tramping on a grave, if not worse. I have no criticism of Wartime Housing. I know that in Peterborough we simply had to have war-time houses or some other kind of housing. We would, of course, have preferred permanent houses to be built under National Housing, but we were given to understand that these houses put up under the war-time scheme would be moved or torn down within six months after the war or as soon as possible thereafter. I hope that will happen.
I also hope that in the future Wartime Housing will not put their houses in restricted districts, because that always causes friction and hard feeling not only toward Wartime Housing but toward the war effort in general.
I have here a letter in regard to putting these sheds on the victory gardens which I

Another point that I want to mention in regard to Wartime Housing is that there have been requests from time to time from soldiers' families to occupy these houses. I hope that in the future soldiers' families will not have to go through as much red tape as they have had to do in the past to occupy one of these houses.
Another thing that has come to my attention is the protest that has been made by municipalities right across this country in regard to the smallness of the allowance which the government makes to the municipalities for taxes on wartime housing. It is absolutely too small an allowance to provide for police protection, schools, supply of water and other services which the cities give. Wartime Housing and the government should see to it that in the future the municipalities are reimbursed a little more adequately than they have been in the past.
In regard to Wartime Housing staff houses, I had a return brought down on April 8 of this year. The second question which was answered by the return was as follows:
On what terms are they (the concessionaires) allowed the use of the staff houses?
That is the concessionaires who cater to the different Wartime Housing staff houses in Canada. The answer to that question was:
The agreement between concessionaires and Wartime Housing Limited is generally to the effect that for a fee of 5 per cent of the gross income the concessionaires operate the cafeterias for the account of Wartime Housing Limited. The concessionaire is limited to a maximum fee

War Appropriation-Supplies-Housing
of 5 per cent. Out of this fee, he must supply the necessary skilled staff, supervision and the services of his head office. . . .
The head office might be in Torqnto, where I believe it is. That is all he has to supply, just his own head office, except perhaps one man. The answer goes on:
There have been variations of the foregoing agreement, namely, at the Prince Rupert and Hamilton staff houses, but these are being standardized in accordance with the above.
Question 3 was this:
Do they pay for (a) breakage and repairs to equipment; (b) wages of the dining room and kitchen staff?
The answer to the first part of the question was:
(a)	The breakage and repairs to equipment are for the account of' Wartime Housing Limited as part of the cost of food service.
In other words, the concessionaire does not have to pay for breakages, and of course does not have to supply kitchen utensils or anything else. The rest of the answer was:
(b)	The wages of the dining room and kitchen staff are for the account of Wartime Housing Limited as part of the cost of food preparation.
In other words, the concessionaire does not have to pay anything at all toward the upkeep of the staff house diningroom. I would ask the minister to explain why the concessionaires were allowed to cater on a contract like that. I understand that in Peterborough alone there is a loss of $5,000 a month.
Another return I got shows the number of men or women occupying these different staff houses. In Peterborough, on December 31 of last year

I do not think the figures have changed since then-there were, according to this return, only ninety people in this staff house.
I suggested when we were on the army estimates that perhaps staff houses could be used for military hospitals. I think it would be wise if that could be done.
I have here another return, dated May 14, 1943, regarding rates charged for meals, single rooms, double rooms, et cetera, in staff houses; and Fort William, has preference over all other places in Canada. In Fort William you can get a single room for $12 or a double room for $10 a month. The lowest rate at any other staff house in Canada is $3.50 a week for a single room or $2.50 for a double room. Why is Fort William given preference in the matter of rates? In many instances these rates are too high, and that is why men will not occupy rooms in the staff houses.

I do not believe we have yet had particulars as to the distribution of the amount-slightly over thirty million
dollars-expended over the past year in the different provinces. I raise this matter also with a view of placing before the minister a situation which prevails in the town of Davidson, Saskatchewan, within my own constituency. The result is that housing is almost impossible to get for those who are attached to the staff or connected with the development. There is another matter I wish to draw to the attention of the minister. To-day the purpose of government departments should be as far as possible to reduce unnecessary expenditures to the minimum. It gives the Minister of Finance power to acquire by way of lease from the owners thereof not more than forty suitable dwellings located in the city of Ottawa for the purpose of converting the buildings into multiple housing units. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) has never appreciated the difference between the national housing plan and Wartime Housing Limited, the purpose of each and how each operates; otherwise I do not think he would be constantly comparing the two plans. The national housing plan has been in existence for a good many years; I believe it was put in workable form about 1936 and it has been carrying on since then. Under that plan a private owner desiring to build a home can 
obtain certain financial assistance from the dominion government; or as my hon. friend says, partly from loan companies and partly from the dominion government. The loan companies take a certain part of the risk and the dominion government a certain' part; the private owner makes a certain, original investment, and the house is built by the owner. That opportunity has at all times been available to those desiring to build and own their own homes. Right through the war it has been, and is to-day, available, as it has been for several years. Nothing that Wartime Housing has done interferes in any way with the national plan, but it takes care of a different need for housing.
In comparing the administration of the two plans, the hon. member is again comparing two different things. The national housing administration is in the position of a mortgage company. It is not responsible for building the house, but is simply responsible for the loan making sure that the house is a desirable house on which to place a loan, and in seeing thfct the details of the loan are worked out. On the other hand, Wartime Housing Limited actually builds houses. It acquires land, and arranges for the sewer, the water and all the facilities; it buys the material and builds the houses, and after a house is built it operates the housing project. National Housing is not responsible for collecting rents or anything of that sort. It must, of course, intervene if the payments on the house are not made over a period, but it is not its job to go each month and collect rents and in general to administer the property, whereas, in the case of Wartime Housing, its job is to collect rents and generally to administer the project. So that in comparing the cost of administration my hon. friend is comparing two totally different operations, operations that are not comparable in any way.
As to the job of Wartime Housing, hon. members know that Canada has been building and enlarging her industrial structure. Large plants have been built in certain communities and there has been a considerable influx of population to these communities. The shift in population is probably temporary, at least in part. There has been a temporary need for housing in order to permit these factories to operate. The function of Wartime Housing, and the only function for which it was originally designed, is to enable the factories and war plants to function by providing houses for the men and women brought in to be employed in these plants.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to discuss this question of war-time housing because it affects the constituency which I have the honour to represent and which is located in the suburbs of Toronto. A peculiar thing is happening in the Toronto metropolitan area. Within the last ten years the population of Toronto proper has increased only five per cent, whereas the population of the surrounding municipalities has increased by over one-third. The result has been that large areas in Toronto are blighted by having numbers of houses which are unsuitable for renting or for subdivision, in many ways unsuitable for habitation at all. The shift in population is to the outskirts where new factories are being established.
Another peculiar thing is happening in Toronto. In the city itself the shift is to tenant rather than owner occupancy, whereas in the outskirts the shift is the other way. I am quoting Controller Saunders' article which appeared in News and was taken from a recent bluebook published by the city. The assessment commissioner's report shows that in 1934 owner-occupied homes numbered 61,552 as against 58,764 in 1942. The same report shows that tenant-occupied homes in 1934 numbered 45,000 and increased) in 1942 to 49,983. This is a significant increase and shows the direction of the trend in the city.
Recently a questionnaire was sent out to employees of the John Inglis company asking whether they had any complaint to make about their present housing conditions. I understand that out of 10,000 questionnaires sent out, only ten reported that their conditions of housing were bad. I do not know whether that is true, but I got it from reliable sources. In my opinion this wartime housing which is being put up in the outskirts of Toronto is an extremely dangerous development. I have no great criticism to make of it as a purely war-time development, but there should be a definite agreement that these houses will be removed1 after the war is over. Otherwise we shall have around Toronto a belt of slums similar to what was built after the last war.
I can remember at that time when farms were subdivided into thirty- to fifty-foot lots which were sold for a small down payment. There were few if any building restrictions, and in many cases jerrybuilt shacks were built. The builder hoped to make a profit on these Their history has, however, been extremely sad. They built on speculative

War Appropriation-Supplies-Housing
land and employed speculative builders, with the net result that the purchasers received very poor value for the money they invested. Two things happened: either the owners felt that they could not afford to continue with the building of the house they started) after the last war. or they wished to move to better jobs elsewhere and found that their commitments, either to pay for the lots or to pay for what had been done already on their houses, was a millstone round their necks, and in many cases they were tied to what has proved to be a wasting asset, and in many cases a positive liability.
Then something else happened. The municipalities in the suburban districts of Toronto found that they had1 to provide sewage, fire, water, police and other services, and their tax rates, based upon land values, rose considerably. The assessment rose, also, and there were large belts of farms surrounding these developments where the farmers found that their taxes made it absolutely impossible for them to continue profitable farming; in many cases they were made bankrupt. To a great extent the land on which these houses were built during the depression came back to the municipalities for taxes, and of course the mortgage money was lost. Taxation mounted to such an extent that it was futile for men to endeavour to own their own homes; economically it was wrong. Then the municipalities got into difficulties, on account of unpaid taxes; one by one they went into receivership with the province, and they are only now recovering.
I want to warn the minister and the country about this wartime housing. If it goes on without definite checks and safeguards we shall have the same condition we found at the end of the last war, only greatly intensified. I believe in the Leaside district some of these houses are built twenty-nine to the acre, and in Toronto township there are more than thirty to the acre, while modern planning would never consider building more than about eight or, at the most, nine houses to the acre. These are the dangers that we are running into; these are the dangers I see, and I want to warn the minister and Wartime Housing Limited that unless care is taken we shall have built around the city of Toronto the greatest belt of slums, the greatest depressed area, we have ever had in Canada. We must take very great care that we do not bring about that result.

After the war is over and these houses have served their purpose, we shall be glad to sit down with any municipality and hear what they want to do with the houses, but just now we are not going to make any other arrangements about them. Most of them are built on an agreement that the houses will be removed after the war. In the

If the tenants could make some arrangement with the municipality they could even at this late date go ahead and put a solid foundation under the house, which would go a long way toward' preserving it. Otherwise you are penalizing the tenants.

What arrangements have been made for the payment of taxes by Wartime Housing? Is there a blanket arrangement applying all over Canada, or do the arrangements vary from city to city, particularly with regard to school taxes?
It is the same arrangement all across Canada.
That is $24 for a two-room house and $30 for a three-room house?
That is right.
I see it is estimated that the salvage value will be about twenty-five per cent of the price of the house.

I do not know about that; it all depends. As I say, we built them for the war. After the war we shall have a look. We built them during the war to tear down. The rents are fixed so that without interest on the investment they will write themselves off in ten years. If the war lasts for four or five years, they will be half written off, and we shall have a look at that situation. My feeling is that, wdiatever happens, these houses will be used; if not on the sites they are now, they will be moved into the country. I would not worry too much about the salvage, because I think they are the type of house that can be salvaged.

I notice that large quantities of plywood are being used in the construction of these houses. How are these supplies obtained, by contract or tender; how much was purchased up to the end of March, 1943, and what price was paid?

We have used no plywood in houses for the last year. Some may have been used in the earlier houses. I have not the information my hon. friend wants. Of course plywood has got in short supply. It is used for many war purposes, and when it could not be had we got other material.
Has the minister any idea how much was used up to a year ago?

It was a price which the department negotiated. All materials bought in quantity are bought at prices fixed by the Department of Munitions and Supply. How much we used, or what the price was, I could not say offhand.

I have one question which, I think comes under this item. I have received numerous inquiries regarding boxes and crates of war material lying on the sidings, particularly in the east end of Toronto and Scarborough. I am told by men who work in the railway yards that some of that material has been lying there for more than a year and a half. I understand the difficulties of shipping, but people who are buying Victory bonds and paying taxes for the production of these goods are anxious to know whether large quantities of them have now become obsolete. There is plenty of evidence that material inside the boxes is rusting, and people in the Toronto area, at least, are very much concerned over the large quantities of material which apparently are not being moved from these yards. A certain change is taking place. Anyone who passes these yards in the train can see boxes there which have become weather-beaten during the months that have passed. The same boxes remain there month after month. I am told some of them have been there nearly two years. Would the minister care to make a statement on that situation?

I can relieve the mind of my hon. friend at once. None of the material piled along railway sidings is obsolete. The fact of the matter is that we accumulate material in Canada between operations.

Canada is in itself an arsenal from which goodis are moved direct to theatres of war. We had quite an accumulation of stores in Canada prior to the movement into North Africa. At that time everything we had was cleared away. At the present time there is quite an accumulation of vehicles. Only now are we beginning to move with a good deal of rush. But those accumulations take place; they are a part of the game, and we have no objection to having Canada used as a storehouse for the theatres of active war. There is no store piled along the tracks that has been there for two years-I can assure my hon. friend of that-nor for one year. But at the present time there is considerable storage of motor vehicles along the tracks. Perhaps the accumulation is the largest there has ever been. But probably in the next three or four months it will be back again to well below normal. It is a part of the transportation business, and nothing to get alarmed about.
I think the important part of the minister's statement, and that part which I am particularly glad to hear, is that none of that material has become obsolete-
That is correct.
-and that all will be used.
Yes.

I wish to ask the minister some questions regarding shipbuilding, and .'particularly with relation to the Toronto Shipbuilding Company. I have here a return tabled March 17, 1943, sessional paper No. 212, concerning the Toronto Shipbuilding Company. In brief, it says that sixteen minesweepers were built by this company, the last being in September 16, 1942. I understand that these ships were nearly all fabricated before the government took the plant over and it became a government plant. I pass the Toronto Shipbuilding Company yard practically every day I am in Toronto, and I see the same ships there that have been there since last summer: I know them quite well. I was informed that you could not take those ships down to the St. Lawrence or to tidewater on account of ice conditions, but the ships are still there, the same ships which were there most of last summer, and1 it is nearly July. What is the matter at the Toronto Shipbuilding Company yards? There have been frequent reports of labour unrest. One, which is quite interesting, appears in to-day's paper; I shall read it to the minister.

The last time I happened to be at the Toronto Shipbuilding Company yards, or rather next door, at the Toronto Elevators, a game of quoits was being played on the deck of one of these ships. I understand that that is not uncommon. What is holding up these Algerine mine-sweepers? Is it lack of labour? Is it lack of skilled help? They can be launched all right: why are they still there? How many can we expect will get to tidewater this year? What is behind the continual stories of bickerings and labour unrest in this plant? I see in to-night's newspaper:
Must quit C.I.O. if they want jobs back
Toronto, June 21.- (C.P.)-Officials of the Toronto Shipbuilding Company said last night that nearly 300 employees dismissed Friday after taking part in a work stoppage Thursday "are not back at work."
"They're through," said the officials adding that the company would consider to.-day whether the men would be accepted again for employment.
"If they start, they will first have to dissociate themselves from the C.I.O.," said an official. "They are in the minority."
That is a most peculiar statement.

Whose statement is it? It
is not mine, is it?

It is a Canadian Press
statement in to-day's Citizen.
I do not know who gave it to the Canadian Press.

All I know is that it is by the Canadian Press and it quotes an official. It is a most peculiar statement concerning this shipbuilding yard, coming on top of the other press statements that they were short of labour and the fact that there was a half-page in the Globe and Mail some weeks ago stating that there was such a Shortage, and the further fact that I asked the minister for naval services a question in this regard and he said they were not short of labour. Now there is a strike. Why are these people playing quoits on the deck? What is the matter? Why cannot the work be finished? Do they lack engines? We hear of the John Inglis company building all the engines they need. Do these people need wiring or equipment, or do they need the necessary skill? I ask the minister in all fairness, because I know he is trying to do a job: what is the matter at this plant?

There is nothing wrong in
the Toronto shipyard. Its production record is good. My hon. friend knows that ships
cannot be delivered in the winter, but deliveries of ships in the last month have been satisfactory. We do not give delivery figures

War Appropriation-Supplies
of naval vessels and we have never done so, for reasons which my hon. friend will appreciate. There is a little labour trouble at the moment and I gave a statement on it earlier in the day. The whole fact of the matter is that it is an A.F. of L. yard, fully unionized by the A.F. of L. A rival union, the C.I.O., under the direction of Mr. Millard of the steel workers' union, is attempting to organize the yard, which is perhaps all right, but he held a meeting of his cohorts in the yard in working time, which, we thought, is going a little far. Certainly it is a flagrant violation of the agreement with the management and its workers. Therefore the workers who took part in the meeting were dismissed for a breach of the rules of the yard. The statement my hon. friend read was not put out by any official; I can assure him of that. If the men wish to return to work individually, they will be employed and it will not be necessary for them to separate themselves from their union affiliation. But it is necessary, as long as the yard is organized by the A.F. of L., that the rules that govern the present agreement shall govern all workers, and if there is a jurisdictional dispute it will be held outside the gates.

I did not intend to discuss
this particular matter, but the minister has made a statement which is certainly not in accordance with the facts, and I know that he wishes to be fair and to be informed on matters of this sort. I happen to have been in Toronto over the week-end, specifically on the matter of which the minister speaks. On Friday afternoon I received a telephone call from one of the union men at that particular plant-
What union?
The steel workers' union.

Is it affiliated with the
C.I.O.?
I will explain that.
Have they a plant agreement?

No. The minister does not
understand this matter as well as I know he would like to. I am interested in shipbuilding, and I am interested in every shipbuilding yard in this country operating at the present time.
My hon. friend is personally an official of the steel workers' union?
No.
What office do you hold?
Oh, no.
You are, are you not?

No; I belong to the mine workers. As I was saying, the telephone conversation I had wras to the effect that there was a possibility, on account of the action of the company in dismissing 289 skilled men who are necessary to that plant, that there would be serious interruption to the work of that yard, and that if there was anything I could do about it, it would be appreciated.
I therefore brought the matter up in the house and the minister made a short statement. What this union official who telephoned to me-and it was not Millard-anticipated, took place. There were 1,200 men idle in the yard on Saturday for the purpose of holding a protest meeting in sympathy with the men who were dismissed. I went to Toronto specifically to attend that meeting. I met with the executive of the steel workers' union who were directly involved in the dispute and got the background of the whole situation. I advised them that they should return to work and that under no circumstances at this time should there be any interruption in the activities of that yard. If the management did wrong in dismissing the men without consultation with the selective service, I pointed out that interrupting the job would not remedy matters, since it precluded the possibility of any negotiations while there was a stoppage of any description in the yard. The men on Saturday morning decided to go back to their jobs, which they did, but the 289 men stayed out. This is what happened in that yard. No meeting was held in the yard, as the minister states. His information in that regard is wrong. The yard is partly organized under craft 7, and there is no interference with the section of the yard that is organized under contract. But a large percentage of the men in the yard who are new war workers are not organized and are not protected by agreements which the craft unions have in the yard, and after carrying on for two years, the men who are now attempting to organize came to the conclusion that they must have some bargaining agency to care for their interests. A representation has been made to the Department of Labour for a vote. They have gone through the machinery provided by government. and last Friday when the 289 men were dismissed this is what took place. It was not a meeting and there was practically no time of the company's involved. At the end of a shift the men are allowed ten minutes to change their clothes and wash up, and on the termination of their shift they utilized that ten minutes to go to the manager's office and ask him if he would cooperate with the Department of Labour and the section of the
War Appropriation-Supplies

union who were endeavouring to get a ballot, and sanction the taking of a ballot. The Minister of Labour had informed them previously that he was favourable to a ballot in that yard to determine the bargaining agency if all concerned were satisfied. The management were not satisfied and they were holding up that function of the Department of Labour. That is the only demonstration that took place.
Are the A.F. of L. men satisfied?

I do not know whether they are, because they do not enter into the picture anyway, seeing that they have their own agreements for their own crafts. They are not taking part in this dispute, and quite naturally if their field was being invaded they would not be satisfied. But the fact of the matter is that the men who are attempting now to get a spokesman for themselves have no agreement and have not had one for two years.
I have no intention of going into the background of this dispute. I sat in and heard these men, discuss this matter. Twenty-five per cent of the men involved are ex-servicemen of this war. They find it hard to understand the attitude of the Toronto Shipbuilding company, particularly since it is a crown company. Some of them have been critical about this. I saw the memorandum which was prepared yesterday, a copy of which I believe has been sent to the minister, and this contains some rather serious accusations against the management of the plant. It is claimed that there has been a wastage of public money.
I did not intend to go into this matter to-night because I wanted to discuss it personally with the minister, but it has been brought before the committee. These 289 men who are idle are skilled welders, mechanics and men of that description, and I think the minister would be well advised to order them back to work and to examine the background of this situation. Some of the stories I heard with respect to the management would- certainly leave room for investigation. The minister or some of the departmental officials should have gone down to meet these men. These things do not spring up by themselves; there is always something behind them. There are always two sides to'a story.
This company is under the control of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and no local manager should be permitted to take the precipitous action which was taken in this case and which has created this situation. If he does, he should be talked to at least. The

Minister of Munitions and Supply should have been consulted, and selective service regulations should have been adhered to. Under those regulations I think these men have a claim for the wages they have lost by reason of this dispute. It is not right to say that these men can go back to work individually. They could not go back yesterday.' After these men had terminated their meeting at two o'clock Saturday evening and had come to a sensible understanding, they found that they could not get in touch with the manager of the plant. Regardless of the fact that there were 1,200 men off the job, no one at the plant would talk to them and they could not get the manager's home telephone number. He did not want to be bothered. I think the manager of a plant maintained by the taxpayers of this country has no right to consider that he is too big to talk to people who are just as important to the plant as he is.
I think any man in this country has a right to belong to the organization he wants to. It is not in, accordance with the regulations with respect to discrimination when the manager of a plant walks up to a man who has decided to join a particular organization and tells him that he must take off that button or ribbon which designates his organization or get off the grounds. That has been, done to men at this plant who are endeavouring to have the steel workers act as their bargaining agent. You can get man after man to make an affidavit that that is the way in which he has been treated by the officials of this plant. The memorandum sent to the minister is self-explanatory. It was prepared by men who have been working on the job for the last two or three years and who know what is going on.
There is reason for investigation of the Toronto shipbuilding yards. They are not turning out ships, and in some eases those that they have turned out have had to be rebuilt. There is rank inefficiency. I believe the minister wants to get the job done, he wants to be reasonable and fair in these matters, but someone should examine into the whole situation. These men should be ordered back to work. They are quite satisfied; their only complaint as far as the government is concerned is in connection with their representations to the Minister of Labour. He agreed that a ballot could be taken provided all concerned were satisfied, but the Toronto Shipbuilding company were not satisfied.
No meeting was held in the yard on company's time and sponsored by the steel workers' union. Charles Millard, the man the minister mentioned, was most concerned to

War Appropriation-Supplies
get these men back on the job. Mr. Sifton, the organizer for the steel workers at that plant, stood up and told these men that in no circumstances must they be off the job. He told them that they must get back on the job and give those who were interested an opportunity of ironing this out with the proper department under the proper regulations. That was their approach to the problem. However, the men had been antagonized by pin-headed foremen who have no business being in a position where they must handle men. Their only function appears to be to stand around and snoop and listen and accuse the .men wanting to join an organization where they will have a spokesman to speak for them on matters of wages and conditions. Some of these men who were casualties of this war and who are now employed at the plant stood up in that meeting yesterday and wanted to know where the democracy was they had been fighting for. They contended they had made their contribution and were trying to work, but they were not allowed to work by people who neither had rendered service nor were capable of giving service in the position in which they were employed. I want to sit down with the minister some time and talk this matter over with him, because there are factors in the dispute which I would not want to discuss publicly.

Disguise it as you like, this is the standard technique for the C.I.O. crashing a plant where the contract is held by the A.F. of L. A small group start milling around demanding votes, and members of my hon. friend's party go down and agitate and make speeches. If there is an illegal strike or overruling of a vote or anything of that sort, my hon. friend is right there to take the side against law and order, as he was in this case. This is a case where the contract is held by a reputable international union, and my hon. friend was down there supporting the minority who wanted to crash the plant and upset the present contract.
I can hardly credit that statement coming from the minister.
It is quite obvious.
It is 100 per cent wrong. How many of the men employed in that plant are covered by the contract?
A considerable majority.
There is not a considerable maj ority.
I will get the figures.

You should get the figures on that. I want the minister to take back his
statement that I am on the side that is against law and order. I am ready to put my record alongside the minister's in that respect from the time I was fifteen years old.
Would the hon. member like me to give him a list of the illegal strikes where he has been advising the striker to act against government regulations?
Yes, I would.
I shall be glad to look that up.

I want to tell the minister that since the outbreak of the war there has never been a strike in this country that was called by the employees of any plant. If you will examine your regulations as they exist at the present time, you will find that they make it impossible for anything but a walkout to occur. That is what has taken place. The Minister of Labour shakes his head. If he reads and examines and goes through the regulations he will find that to be true. Before any body of workers employed in a plant in this country can obtain redress for any grievance they must first make application for a conciliation board, and before any application for a conciliation board is granted they are compelled to take a strike vote.
That is only nominal.

Just a moment. You must
recognize this, that there is no strike in Canada. Eighty-five per cent of the workers of this country are not organized; they have absolutely no knowledge of trades unionism or its functions, or the road they have to travel. When somebody gets up and tells them there is to be a strike vote taken and that this is to be done for the purpose of redressing their grievances, immediately you take a vote you sow the seeds of a strike in the minds of those uninitiated men; you plant the germs of a strike, and you place the average organizer or the man trying to handle the difficulty in a situation which he cannot control. Why was I in Toronto on Saturday? I was there because the people who telephoned and asked me to go to Toronto said, "These men may listen to you; they will not listen to us." I sat in with the executive, the rank and file of the men off the job. They had a pertinent grievance that has been agitating them for two years. The organizers had lost control; the men were not listening to them. I sat with those men for two hours, persuading them as to what they should do in order to legalize themselves and iron out this grievance through the medium of the machinery provided by the government.
War Appropriation-Supplies

Then the minister rises in his place and tells me I am on the side that is against law and order, that I am trying to promote this, that and the other thing. I tell the minister that I want to win this war; I have already helped to fight one war. It may be that I want to win this war for a different reason from what the minister thinks, but I am not letting anything I can control interfere with the winning of the war. I know the aftermath is too serious. I defy the Minister of Munitions and Supply or anyone else in this house to show that since the outbreak of this war I have gone to a plant or a factory from one end of this country to the other and advocated a strike or a stoppage of work. The reverse has been true. I went to Sudbury; I went to Kirkland Lake; I went all over this country, and I advised the men that the only sensible and safe road to travel was to build up their membership to the point where they would be safe when a ballot was taken at the particular plant. The strike is an obsolete weapon. I know enough about the labour movement to realize that there has never been a strike won in the history of that movement, on the question of recognition. You cannot win; I know that, and it is foolish to think about it. My mission in Toronto was to talk to the uninitiated workers in this plant who perhaps do not understand the situation as well as I do. It is not the technique of the C.I.O. to promote strikes; no such thing. The reverse is true; they are forced into these things.
Then how is it that eighty-five per cent of all the time that has been lost in this country since the beginning of the war has been owing to the C.I.O. ?

The answer is very simple.
The A.F. of L. unions are craft unions and are well established.

They are not all craft
unions; how about the mine workers?

They are not in the A.F.
of L. at the present time.

The machinists are not
a craft union.

If the Minister of Labour will wait a minute I will give the Minister of Munitions and Supply a little information; there may be no need to give it to the Minister of Labour. The craft unions are well established. The unions of the A.F. of L. are craft unions now; the ones that were not craft unions broke away from the A.F. of L. when John Lewis and Bill Green disagreed 
in the United States. Those unions are well organized; they have contracts and leadership, but they stop there. The difficulty was that until about four years ago the mass-production industries of the United States and Canada were not organized. There was no unionism in steel or all those other mass-production industries at all. That was why Green and Lewis quarrelled; then the C.I.O. was formed in the United States, and they are fighting to establish what the A.F. of L. have had for twenty years. The same thing applies in Canada. In these other unions there is no disturbance. They are established; they have machinery, and there is no reason for a fight. But in all the mass-production industries they are trying to establish something that has been recognized in every other country in the world for the last fifty years; that is all.
That is why we are having this scrap. And what are they asking for? You have no objection to the manufacturers' association getting together. That is fine; no one is against that. You have no objection to the mining association getting together; they can come in here and meet you en bloc, and they represent the whole set-up.
I have no objection to labour getting together. The objection I have is to one faction of labour fighting another and losing time which should be devoted to the war.
I have the same objection; I think it should not be, but neither the minister nor I can do very much about that at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: What about coal?
That has been organized for a good many years.
What about it?
That is one of the industries in which there has been a tremendous loss of time.

Yes, and there has been very good reason for it. The Secretary of State will remember also that last summer the mining industry of Canada was working only three days a week. Why were we losing time then? It was the fault of the employers, on account of a lack of organization. We cannot help the row that is going on in the United States; that is their business. Evidently John Lewis thinks his men are entitled to more money. There has been very little lost time in Canada by reason of trouble in union circles.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I am afraid I cannot entirely agree with that statement. We did have much trouble.
Where?
In Cape Breton, where the hon. member comes from.
What was the trouble?

The trouble was a slowdown on the one hand and absenteeism on the other.
Mr, GILLIS: What was the reason for it?
It was purely a jurisdictional fight within the union.

No such thing. Sit down for a moment andi I will tell you what was wrong at that time. I know this is all out of order, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to tell the Secretary of State what was the trouble in Nova Scotia.
It was a fight inside the union itself.
No-well, to a certain extent it was.
To a great extent.

But that was not the basic trouble. We have gone through that twice in Nova Scotia; we went through it in 1925, and the cause of the difficulty was quite apparent to most of us. You were facing a provincial election. The mine workers of Nova Scotia are a potent factor in provincial elections, and you got manipulations from the inside to disrupt that whole organization so that it would not be a factor in that provincial election. That was seventy-five per cent of your trouble, manipulated trouble on the inside of the union to disrupt the whole thing. That was what happened. The men were taken for a ride.
I am sorry I had to take up this time, but I am not the kind of person who can sit quietly and just take the sort of accusation the Minister of Munitions and Supply made across the floor. I tried to be helpful in the Toronto situation; I wanted to discuss it with the minister. There is nothing wrong there. Send those men back to work; that is all. They were dismissed illegally. You need them in that plant. Make an investigation into that plant, as to its management; you owe that much to the taxpayers of Canada. You are responsible. If those men want a vote in that plant, that is democracy. They are quite prepared to take a ballot. They are not talking anarchy, communism or dictatorship. The ballot is the basis of democracy; so let the
men settle it on that basis. I do not think Mr. Arnold, who is an employee of the federal government, and managing that plant, has any right to say that anyone in the plant should belong to this, that or anything else. That is something the individual must determine for himself, and that is all there is to that dispute. It is a matter of deciding whether we are prepared to give the people _ of this country democracy, the thing they are fighting for overseas. If we are not going to do it now, then I am very much afraid of what the situation will be when this war is over.

Before we close the books on that subject, may I say the objection was not that the men belonged to a certain union. They could belong to any union they like, and I am certain no foreman on the job told them differently. The objection was that they held meetings on the company's time.
They did not; that is not right.

That is the fact given to me. That was the reason for the dismissal, and that is a perfectly good reason for dismissal. The men can do their organizing and hold their meetings outside the yard, and outside business time.

I agree with that, and I say that if they held meetings in the yard on company time for organizational purposes, the dismissal was justified. But that is not so. We could get many men in the plant who would take their affidavit that the foreman would walk up to them and tell them to "get that button off your coat"-or else.
I do not wish to get into this discussion, but I know that there are American Federation of Labour organizations in that plant.
Yes, certainly there are.

Not long ago one of
the international representatives of the American Federation of Labor came to my office, and told me that the pot was boiling there, and that there was a scrap between the two organizations. But if it had not been for the closed shop in the plant they could consolidate things, and there would not be any difficulty. I told him the viewpoint of the government with respect to the closed shop was that it was in contradiction of P.C. 2685, and we did not feel that a man should be denied the right to go to work, or that before he should go to work he should join any particular trades union.
War Appropriation-Supplies

I think it can. be fairly said that I know something about the difficulties of dealing with green membership. But do not forget there is also green leadership in this country.
Hear, hear.

An>d I want to say to
my hon. friend that very few disputes have gone off the track since the war broke out. The government and its conciliatory machinery cannot always be wrong. I am frank to admit that we are human, and that we do make mistakes. But I do not think it is fair to say that every time somebody else makes a mistake it should be put on the doorstep of the Minister of Labour, whether it be a federal minister or a provincial minister.
The leaders in this situation in Toronto- and if they cannot lead they should not be leaders-knew the steps which were necessary to bring that situation, which they thought was dangerous, to a successful conclusion. But no, they waited until the fellows were out on the street. I know it is the easiest thing in the world, as I have no doubt every hon. member knows, to tell people they are right when they are wrong. That is the easiest thing one can do. While I do not hold any brief for any of the employers in this country, yet it has been my experience-and I have probably had as much experience as my hon. friend, and I do not make that statement in any critical sense-to find that trades union agreements are based on character. That comes first, last, and all the time. A trades union agreement is not a legal document, nor is it a legal document in Great Britain. There are some who would try to make it a legal document, but it is not. It is a yardstick arrived at between employers and employees. There is a duty on both sides to make that instrument function. I know some believe that is not very helpful; but it has been my experience that those organizations based on character do not need laws. We can see that all the powerful organizations in this country and in the United States have lasted because their policies and purposes have been functioning on that true, simple fact.
I think my hon. friend will agree with me that when sometimes you get mistakes in leadership on either side, whether it be on the part of employees or employers, you cannot lay it at the feet of the conciliation machinery of the respective governments of the country concerned. If there were more forbearance on both sides it would be better. That is something which cuts both ways, and if there were more forbearance it would be much better
I Mr. Mitchell.]
in this country and in the United States; because, whether we like it or not, there is a struggle between two organizations for membership. They poach on one another, I suppose, as they have done in the United States.

Would the minister answer
a question?
Yes.

That plant has been operating since the outbreak of the war. The A. F. of L. union that is in the plant, and that has contracts with its own people, has had that field completely to itself up until the last three months, has it not? Now, if the A. F. of L. did not include the whole yard, why have they not done so in the last two and a half years? That is the point. The steel workers were invited to organize themselves, and they were not protected by the agreement. That is the crux of the whole matter.

I wish to have that clear. I am not criticizing the steel workers. The hon. member will have to agree with me that I have taken the stand, since I have been Minister of Labour-and I think earlier ministers have; and this is the same position taken in Great Britain and in the United States- that I did not think it was the duty of any government to send in conciliators when the men are on what is known as an illegal strike.
That is true.
On what?

When the men are on an illegal strike. When that is gone, everything is gone. If hon. members on the opposition side of the house were sitting where I am sitting, they would see that you have to have some measure of control. The government, by its very nature, is charged with a responsibility to the state, and it cannot permit a group of individuals, whether they be employers or employees, to act at variance with government policy. You find that in connection with the Minister of Munitions and Supply, for instance, when in his judgment he finds it necessary to put in a controller to take charge of a certain industry. That is often done.
We have not yet reached the stage where we have put controllers into these organizations. But if we are to develop responsible trades union leadership, that has to be done. There is no other alternative to it, irrespective of the political party in power.
Those problems exist. They exist in every country in the world in which we find the democratic style of government. And where

democracy is in operation, that is the price we pay for freedom. I realize that the hon. member is trying to get these people back to work.
Did the company obey the law in this instance?

I saw the manager of the company. Perhaps I have not as much knowledge about this as the hon. member for Cape Breton South, but I think it is not within the realm of proper operation of any industry for people to hold meetings in a plant during working hours. That is generally recognized in the day to day operation of any industry.

I would remind the minister there was no meeting held in that plant on the company's time. It is not correct to say that there was. The Minister of Munitions and Supply is under the impression that there is a contract in that yard which embraces the employees; that is not correct, either. The first step should be that the 289 men should be put back in the plant, where they are needed.

May I say that three or four months ago these men came to see me and told me that they were likely to go out on strike, and that they could not continue on account of the inefficiency of the management at this plant, that there was bound to be a strike for that cause alone.
Progress reported.
